scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Though named for Sicily and rooted in 14th-century island poetry, the siciliana became a pan-European Baroque signifier of pastoral grief and melancholy.
This is siciliana. 14th century origins, Baroque to 20th century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Investigations trace the siciliana back to 14th-century poetic-musical compositions inspired by Sicilian folk songs.
It evolved through the Renaissance strambotto and 17th-century recitar cantando before codifying into Baroque instrumental and operatic forms.
The earliest reference to the term regarding a dance appears in Tommaso Garzoni's 1599 work 'La piazza universale di tutte le professioni del mondo'.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Evokes a pastoral, bucolic, and sentimental mood.
In Baroque opera and Classical compositions, it was frequently used to portray grief, lamentation, and rustic scenes.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Performed in a slow 6/8 or 12/8 time signature with lilting, dotted iambic rhythms, usually in a minor key.
Instruments historically used include the violin, flute, harpsichord, strings, organ, guitar, oboe, clarinet, and brass.
Listen for the violin, flute, harpsichord, strings.
The pulse is 6/8 or 12/8.
A slow, lilting compound meter in 6/8 or 12/8, usually in a minor key, featuring dotted iambic rhythms and a rocking accompaniment that evokes a melancholic pastoral atmosphere.

Rhythm pattern: dotted iambic rhythms with frequent placement of the dot on the first of a series of three notes. Instruments: violin, flute, harpsichord, strings, organ, guitar, oboe, clarinet. Vocal style: operatic arias, strambotto structure, lamenting and melancholic texts. Form: ternary form ABA, rondeau, or da capo. Mood: pastoral, bucolic, melancholic, sentimental, tragic. It should sound like this: A slow, lilting compound meter in 6/8 or 12/8, usually in a minor key, featuring dotted iambic rhythms and a rocking accompaniment that evokes a melancholic pastoral atmosphere. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.
